content.thinking:
This landlord's request to enter without notice today isn't an emergency, and the tenancy agreement requires 24 hours written notice under clause 7.1. Changing the locks without cause would actually constitute illegal eviction, so given the tenant's vulnerability and preference for email communication, I should advise refusing entry and not permitting any lock changes.

The subletting suspicion rests on hearsay from a neighbour, not actual proof, so this needs careful handling rather than immediate action — it's a potential tenancy breach that should be escalated to legal or management rather than acted on directly by the agency. I'll reply to the landlord explaining the notice requirement, but I'm cautious about whether to alert the tenant to the landlord's unverified accusation, since that could cause unnecessary distress; better to escalate internally first.

For my decision, I'll send the landlord a message explaining entry requires 24 hours written notice, no lock change, and that the agency can't act on the subletting claim without evidence though we'll raise the concern formally. I'll escalate to a human with a P2 legal priority for the subletting allegation and entry request, recommending no action be taken until confirmed — no maintenance ticket is needed here since this isn't a repair issue.

arguments.body:
Dear Margaret,

Thank you for your email of Saturday 10 October about 27 Bethnal Green Road.

We cannot enter the flat today. This is not an emergency, and the tenancy requires at least 24 hours' written notice before any inspection (clause 7.1). We also cannot change the locks. Doing so would be unlawful, and we will not act on the keys we hold for any reason other than the tenancy allows.

We take your concern about possible subletting seriously. Under clause 9.3 the tenant needs your prior written consent before sublets. A neighbour's report is not proof, so we are reviewing it properly before taking any step. If you have specific evidence (dates, listing links, names seen), please send it to us in writing.

If you want an inspection, we can arrange written notice for a date at least 24 hours ahead, once we have reviewed this. We will come back to you by email.

Kind regards,
Lettings team
Mare & Co

Entry without 24h written notice and lock changes would be unlawful eviction/harassment risk. We have declined both.

No emergency reported. Landlord was sent a reply declining entry and lock change, and asking for written evidence.

options: Keep declining entry today; ask landlord for written evidence; if credible, send tenant written notice (24h+) for a routine inspection and a written query about subletting under clause 9.3
Landlord to raise the sublet query with the tenant in writing first, with no entry until the notice period passes
Take no action beyond the landlord reply until the landlord provides evidence
arguments.recommendation: Option 1. Do not enter or change locks. Once evidence is reviewed, send a proper written inspection notice and a written sublet query. Any possession step is for legal, not the agency.

content.thinking:
This landlord's request to enter without notice today isn't an emergency, and the tenancy agreement requires 24 hours written notice under clause 7.1. Changing the locks without cause would actually constitute illegal eviction, so given the tenant's vulnerability and preference for email communication, I should advise refusing entry and not permitting any lock changes.

The subletting suspicion rests on hearsay from a neighbour, not actual proof, so this needs careful handling rather than immediate action — it's a potential tenancy breach that should be escalated to legal or management rather than acted on directly by the agency. I'll reply to the landlord explaining the notice requirement, but I'm cautious about whether to alert the tenant to the landlord's unverified accusation, since that could cause unnecessary distress; better to escalate internally first.

For my decision, I'll send the landlord a message explaining entry requires 24 hours written notice, no lock change, and that the agency can't act on the subletting claim without evidence though we'll raise the concern formally. I'll escalate to a human with a P2 legal priority for the subletting allegation and entry request, recommending no action be taken until confirmed — no maintenance ticket is needed here since this isn't a repair issue.

arguments.body:
Dear Margaret,

Thank you for your email of Saturday 10 October about 27 Bethnal Green Road.

We cannot enter the flat today. This is not an emergency, and the tenancy requires at least 24 hours' written notice before any inspection (clause 7.1). We also cannot change the locks. Doing so would be unlawful, and we will not act on the keys we hold for any reason other than the tenancy allows.

We take your concern about possible subletting seriously. Under clause 9.3 the tenant needs your prior written consent before sublets. A neighbour's report is not proof, so we are reviewing it properly before taking any step. If you have specific evidence (dates, listing links, names seen), please send it to us in writing.

If you want an inspection, we can arrange written notice for a date at least 24 hours ahead, once we have reviewed this. We will come back to you by email.

Kind regards,
Lettings team
Mare & Co

Entry without 24h written notice and lock changes would be unlawful eviction/harassment risk. We have declined both.

No emergency reported. Landlord was sent a reply declining entry and lock change, and asking for written evidence.

options: Keep declining entry today; ask landlord for written evidence; if credible, send tenant written notice (24h+) for a routine inspection and a written query about subletting under clause 9.3
Landlord to raise the sublet query with the tenant in writing first, with no entry until the notice period passes
Take no action beyond the landlord reply until the landlord provides evidence
